The modern view of retirement needs to stop being seen as the primary goal and finish line for business owners and employees alike.

"Cash out and sail off into the sunset." Is a deeply flawed and concerning perspective that has all but destroyed the intergenerational glue that held nations together since the beginning of time.

It stems from the socialist/communist aspect of "utility" as it relates to members of the whole. When the usefulness (as defined by socialist and communist philosophy) of an individual has reached it's end, then the individual is sent away and discarded where any further utility they have stems from the resources they've maintained, which are drained through assorted means to and for the benefit of the state and other members.

What that currently looks like in reality is someone retires, buys the condo in Florida or Scottsdale, plays 5 rounds of golf a week, goes on a couple of cruises a year, sees their kids and grandkids a couple times a year, and slowly spends down their resources as they turn into pure consumers who spend most if not all of their remaining wealth on healthcare in the last 10 years of their life as their children and grandchildren struggle to establish themselves economically and plant their feet geographically. In only a few years, it's only around the birthdays of the deceased grandparents that their names are even brought up.

In contrast, a strong Christian family that stayed together looks nothing like that. The siblings and the in-laws do life together. Same town, same faith, same dinner table through the week. The grandparents are still a strong presence providing guidance and wisdom, and they offer free childcare. Fathers working alongside sons, and son-in-laws being adopted into the business.  The sibling's families and parents move as one unit with many parts, pulling the same direction. The business, tools, and land do not get sold to fund a ride off into the sunset. The grandchildren know their grandparents, and witness a faithful, fruitful, strong, and economically unified family that is strategically located geographically close to one another. The wealth and purpose stays together, so the next generation plants their feet where the family name already means something. 

This is the living legacy that teaches multiple generations the importance and process of stewarding well that which God has given and building something larger than any one family. 

If you haven't already, shed the hyper-individualism and plan now and begin working to build toward this vision in the decades to come. 

Generational faithfulness is a beautiful thing.

🥊Welterweight Bout: Luis Francischinelli vs Will Rentz

🇧🇷Luis Francischinelli (6-1)
📍Fighting out of California Mixed Martial Arts | Representing Brazil
📏6'6" | Age: 30
🗓Last Fight: LFA 232 (May 15, 2026)
🧨6 KO/TKO, 0 SUB, 0 DEC
⭐Prospect Rating: ★★★☆☆

Francischinelli grew up in Itu, São Paulo, where his mother raised him alongside eight siblings in a household where gym fees were not exactly easy to find. A social project run with the Brazilian kickboxing confederation introduced him to the sport in 2010.

Years later, his mother scraped together enough money for him to travel alone to a South American championship. He left her in tears and returned as a champion. He claims close to 100 kickboxing bouts on the Brazilian circuit before the pandemic brought the competitive calendar to a halt.

At 25, Francischinelli and his then-girlfriend, now his wife, sold their car and motorcycle, contacted strangers for advice, and flew to California. He initially slept in a room behind Black House and shared space with whoever else was there. After hard sparring sessions with Alexander Volkov caught the attention of managers, he eventually moved to California Mixed Martial Arts.

The American chapter remains a calculated gamble. Francischinelli has described himself as a skinny fighter who once competed well below 170 pounds, and the move to California represented a chance to turn a Brazilian kickboxing career that was not paying the bills into something more sustainable.

🇺🇸Will Rentz (8-2)
📍Fighting out of Gracie PAC MMA | Representing United States
📏6'0" | Age: 27
🗓Last Fight: Combat Night Tampa (June 20, 2026)
🧨8 KO/TKO, 0 SUB, 0 DEC
⭐Prospect Rating: ★★☆☆☆

Rentz left Honolulu for the Tampa MMA scene and never really left the gym once he arrived. He fights and coaches out of Gracie PAC, owned by UFC featherweight Billy Quarantillo, who has been in his corner since the beginning of Rentz's professional career.

Quarantillo has also brought him into UFC camps as a sparring partner and had him in his corner for his own fights. Rentz has treated that experience as an education that could not simply be bought. Coaching has become another part of that development. He has said that explaining techniques to other fighters forced him to understand his own wrestling sequences more clearly.

The setbacks have been public. Following a 2023 loss, he framed his response in simple terms: average people are broken by failure. The nickname "Iron Will" comes from that mentality more than any marketing campaign.

His professional career has been almost entirely built around the Florida regional circuit, particularly Cage Fury and local Tampa shows.

👊There is not much about this matchup that inspires confidence.

Francischinelli is one of the more unusual welterweights on the regional scene. At 6'6" with an 83-inch reach, the physical tools are obvious, and he is a fun striker to watch. The problem is that his defensive flaws are just as obvious. He was recently exposed by Jo Piersma at LFA and has only one win since before earning this Contender Series opportunity.

He leaves his chin available, does not offer much on the ground, and relies heavily on his striking advantages.

Rentz is the opposite kind of prospect. His record is polished, but the quality behind it is not particularly impressive. He lost the one time he stepped up against a genuinely credible opponent, getting knocked out by Chris Alvidrez in 2023, and has spent much of the time since beating regional opposition.

He looks better on tape than the résumé suggests, but that is not exactly a high bar.

The physical gap should matter here. Francischinelli's length and striking volume should allow him to find Rentz early, and I expect him to land something before Rentz can turn the fight into the kind of wrestling-heavy contest that could expose Francischinelli's weaknesses.

This feels like a fight where the Contender Series format actually helps Francischinelli. He does not need to show a complete game. He needs to create enough chaos to land the big shot.

✅Luis Francischinelli to win by round 1 knockout

text:
New Injection May Ease Chronic Back Pain | Knowridge

Chronic back pain affects millions of people and can make everyday life difficult. Walking, working, sleeping, driving, or even bending down can become painful, and long-lasting pain can also affect mood and mental health.

One common cause is degenerative disk disease. The spine contains soft disks between its bones that act like cushions, helping absorb pressure and allowing the back to move.

As people get older, these disks can lose water, become thinner, and develop damage. This can lead to pain, stiffness, inflammation, and reduced movement.

Most treatments focus on controlling symptoms. Physical therapy, anti-inflammatory medicines, injections, and painkillers may help, while some people with severe problems eventually need surgery.

Researchers led by Dr. Douglas Beall at Clinical Radiology of Oklahoma have studied a different approach called viable disk allograft supplementation. Instead of only reducing pain, the treatment is designed to improve the condition of damaged spinal disks.

The procedure involves injecting donated disk tissue containing living cells into a damaged disk. Researchers believe this material may help create a healthier environment inside the disk and support tissue repair.

The treatment is minimally invasive and does not require major surgery. Patients receive the injection directly into the affected disk and can generally leave the medical facility the same day.

Early results have been encouraging. In a study of 50 people with chronic lower back pain caused by disk degeneration, about 60% experienced at least a 50% reduction in pain after treatment.

About 70% also had meaningful improvements in physical function. For someone living with chronic back pain, better function could make ordinary activities such as walking, exercising, working, and spending time with family easier.

Another possible advantage is reducing reliance on strong pain medicines, including opioids. These drugs can provide relief but may cause side effects and carry risks when used for long periods.

The treatment is part of regenerative medicine, a growing area of research that aims to help damaged parts of the body repair or restore function. Scientists are studying similar approaches for problems affecting joints, muscles, and other tissues.

However, the treatment is still being studied, and the early findings do not prove that it will work for everyone. Larger and longer studies are needed to determine how long the benefits last, which patients are most likely to improve, and how the treatment compares with other options.

The research on viable disk allograft supplementation was presented at the Society of Interventional Radiology Annual Scientific Meeting. If future studies confirm the results, the approach could eventually offer some people with chronic disk-related back pain another option besides long-term medication or major surgery.

text:
In 1939, six-year-old Willie Nelson dragged an oversized canvas sack through the cotton fields of Abbott, Texas, alongside his older sister, Bobbie. Abandoned by their parents during the Great Depression, the two siblings were raised by their paternal grandparents, who scraped by on whatever the dusty earth could yield. To help keep food on the table, the children were sent into the fields before sunrise.

The work was brutal for a small boy. The sharp dried bolls tore through skin, leaving his fingertips raw and bleeding by mid-morning. Dragging heavy sacks under the relentless Texas sun made his young back ache constantly. He watched older pickers hunch over the rows day after day, their bodies permanently bent and broken by manual labor.

It was in those very rows that Nelson reached a quiet, stubborn decision. He realized that a lifetime in the fields offered only exhaustion and early decline. Looking at his blistered fingers, he swore he would find another way out—and that way was music.

His grandfather had bought him a guitar for six dollars and taught him basic chords, while Bobbie learned the piano. Whenever they could put down their picking sacks, the children practiced. By age ten, Nelson was earning eight dollars playing rhythm guitar in local Bohemian polka bands at Texas dance halls. That single night of music paid more than an entire grueling week of picking cotton.

The memory of Abbott’s cotton rows stayed with him for the rest of his life. Decades later, long after escaping poverty and becoming one of America’s most recognizable musical icons, he never forgot the workers bent over the dirt. Instead of burying those memories, he channeled them into founding Farm Aid in 1985, raising millions to protect family farmers facing financial ruin. The boy who bled in the Texas cotton fields had spent a lifetime making sure others wouldn't be abandoned to the soil.

For anyone who respects the grit behind American music, the untold beginnings of the legends who survived them live here on this page.

Danilo Alves Silva voted in a Brazilian jersey, then went back to his car and came out dressed as ICE.

This was not an American election. Sunday, October 4, was Brazil’s presidential vote, and Miami Dade College’s Kendall campus was one of the U.S. sites where Brazilians living here could cast a ballot in their own country’s race. Silva, 46, of Port St. Lucie, is a Brazilian citizen. He was at that site. Sheriff’s deputies already on the campus watched him move between the buildings in a blue ICE raid jacket, an ICE hat, sunglasses, a face mask, tactical boots, and a handheld radio. Voters told them they thought a real agent was walking their election and that people were going to be deported. When a voter with a camera confronted him, he got aggressive.

He told detectives he was not an agent. He said the outfit was a prop costume from Amazon. He said he had already voted in the jersey, changed in the car, and came back to see how people would react while he recorded on his phone. In the back of the sheriff’s vehicle he told them he would get them paid if they let him go, and that they would regret the arrest and he would come after the detective and everyone on the scene.

He was booked into Turner Guilford Knight on voter intimidation, conspiracy to commit bribery, influencing a public servant, unlawful use of a police insignia, and disorderly conduct. A public defender entered a not guilty plea.

A Brazilian voter put on an Amazon ICE jacket at his own country’s polling site in Miami and offered the deputies money to walk. This is who’s in this country.

Joanna Yakubu, partner of Flight Lieutenant I.S. Bako, one of 25 Nigerian Air Force personnel killed in Tuesday’s aircraft crash in Ondo State, has mourned him in an emotional social media post.

The aircraft, registered NAF 931, crashed into the swamps of Igbokoda in Ilaje Local Government Area while on a routine mission from Benin to Lagos. The NAF said it carried 25 people, five crew members and 20 passengers, and that no survivors were found.

NAF Director of Public Relations and Information, Air Commodore Ehimen Ejodame, said search-and-rescue operations were activated immediately and coordinated with relevant authorities.

The Chief of the Air Staff, Air Marshal Sunday Kelvin Aneke, offered condolences to the families of the victims, calling the crash “a deeply painful moment for the Nigerian Air Force and the nation.”

He assured them of the Service’s full support and ordered a comprehensive investigation into the cause.

Analyst Comments: For those who hold the opinion that the FBI is incapable of stopping a terror attack that they don't plan themselves, the Minnesota case will not exactly help refute that argument. Per the press statements on this case, Mohamud was under investigation for two years...but the violent threats only emerged in September of this year, after he had already turned 18. So far, this seems to be a lone individual speaking with an undercover agent online, who also sold him a rifle and some ammunition before arresting him. Since this investigation lasted two years, it looks like the FBI was trying to entrap a juvenile, and groomed him until he became a legal adult, and they could arrest him. To be sure, the suspect did express radicalization and intent to carry out an attack, but there is no indication that he was actually able to do so without the FBI's help...if he was only talking about these threats to an undercover agent, this is not exactly an indication of a wider terrorist network (or even a particularly capable lone wolf either). Somewhat poignantly, his violent intentions are not out of the ordinary for the Twin Cities. As a reminder, there are many other well coordinated and well funded groups around the city with the means, motive, and opportunity to cause harm; the previous terrorism and fraud concerns throughout the greater Minneapolis area have remained constant threats for years. However, this individual does not appear to have been a part of any coordinated group and despite the good news of one less individual with nefarious intent being out on the street, this is not exactly the Bin Laden-grade takedown that the DoJ is claiming that it is, and the concerns of entrapment will probably grant the suspect a decent legal defense when this case goes to trial.

text:
This is my client population. I work as a therapist in a Psychiatric Residential Treatment Facility (PRTF) 
 in Kansas. It’s an inpatient psychiatric hospital. It’s a psych ward in layman’s terms. Kids who cannot function well in society live with us for months and work to change the behaviors that made them a safety risk either to themselves or others. 

It’s easy to look at the child’s behaviors and think, “Lock the parents up.” I get it, but it’s often more complicated than that. It is true that some chaotic parents live in chaotic situations and pass that chaos onto their children. It is also true that a lot of parents are desperate for their child (and their own lives) to change but don’t know how to make that happen. 

Enter the child welfare and mental health systems.

I was a CPS social worker for 10 years. I looked at some parents and considered that the only way I could get them to extricate themselves from generations of dysfunction was to move in with them. We could refer them to in-home therapy services, but therapy a couple of hours a week isn’t going to cut it for some people. What we have to offer is often inadequate compared to what the parent needs. 

CPS is an entry-level position for frontline workers which means you have the most complex families being cared for by professionals with the least experience. Foster care can be a necessary option (especially for significant parental substance abuse) but out-home-care brings a host of its own problems. It would take much more space than I have here to discuss that. Just know that the last line of defense can become the problem. State governments make terrible parents. 

Just because you go to therapy doesn’t mean you’re receiving good therapy. The term “coping skills” is a slur to me. You can buy a coping skill on Amazon. What people need from a therapist is a way to understand what happened to them, how it impacted them, and a way forward. Families don’t always get that. 

And when I say, “What happened to them,” I do not mean the things we will be using to excuse their behaviors. Allowing people to be a victim in their story (even if they have been victimized) is not compassionate. Over and over and over again, I work with children who have been horribly mistreated and the message is always the same: I’m deeply sorry for all the bad things that have happened to you, but you are responsible for yourself. And I will help you. 

The therapists families turn to for help can be just as avoidant as their clients and equally confused about how to fix what is broken. Don’t think families don’t know that. It’s easy to be intimidated by clients and the magnitude of their problems. It takes a certain kind of person to square up against a kid or their parent who is cussing you up one side and down the other and say, “You are the problem here, and we’re going to keep having this conversation until you change.” 

Talking about coping skills is way easier than fighting through to the root of the problem. This might come as a surprise, but the majority of my clients actually grow to appreciate being called on their stuff, and they recognize that previous therapists who didn’t do it were unhelpful. Why? Because they come to understand that it improved their life. 

A word of caution about the kid in this video: Don’t write him off. He’s got a fighting spirit, and you’d be amazed at the end result if someone can help him and his parent channel it.

THE DEVIL GOT THE MICROPHONE — GHANA SHOULD PAY ATTENTION

“It is done. Hail, Satan!”

Those are not words most Ghanaians expect to hear at the opening of a public meeting.

But perhaps that is precisely why the story deserves our attention.

In Ottumwa, Iowa, former council member and Satanic Temple member Matt Dalbey delivered a Satanic invocation before the city council. He spoke of embracing the “Luciferian impulse” to eat from the tree of knowledge and urged listeners to abandon what he described as the comforting delusions of the past.

Then he finished:

“It is done. Hail, Satan!”

It is easy to dismiss the episode as an American oddity.

That would be a mistake.

The uncomfortable question underneath it has a distinctly Ghanaian relevance:

When government opens a public space for religion, does that space belong to the religious majority—or does it belong to everybody?

Ottumwa’s invocation policy reportedly allows residents to offer prayers regardless of religious affiliation or belief system.

That means the city has to live with an obvious consequence: once government says the microphone is open to religious expression, it cannot simply close it when somebody uses that freedom in a way the majority finds offensive.

That principle is not particularly exotic to Ghana.

Religion is woven deeply into Ghanaian public life. Christian prayers are commonplace at official ceremonies, political gatherings, schools, workplaces and public events. Muslims and members of other faith traditions also participate in the country’s public religious life.

And because Christianity is overwhelmingly visible in Ghanaian society, there is a tendency to treat Christian prayer in public institutions as almost invisible—as though it is simply part of the furniture.

That is precisely when the question of neutrality becomes worth asking.

What happens when the person at the microphone is not Christian?

What happens when it is a Muslim?

An African traditional religious practitioner?

An atheist?

Someone from a smaller religious community?

Or, eventually, someone whose beliefs many Ghanaians find deeply offensive?

Would we still say the public institution should apply the same rule?

That is the real test.

Nobody is being asked to believe in Satanism. Nobody is being asked to approve of Dalbey’s words. And nobody has to pretend that provocative speech is suddenly respectable because somebody calls it religion.

The question is whether government should decide which beliefs are acceptable enough to receive public recognition.

That question matters in Ghana because we have become accustomed to religious expression in official spaces.

Prayers before meetings. Prayers before political events. Prayers at state functions. Invocations before ceremonies.

Most of the time, nobody objects because the words are familiar.

But neutrality is easy when everybody is comfortable.

It becomes difficult when someone stands up and prays to a God—or invokes a belief system—that the majority rejects.

That is where the principle is actually tested.

There is a danger in assuming that because Ghana is a predominantly Christian country, Christian religious expression should automatically receive a special place in every public institution.

Majority culture and government neutrality are not the same thing.

A democratic state does not become more neutral because the majority happens to share the religion being expressed.

And this is where the Iowa story becomes a useful mirror for Ghana.

We should ask ourselves what our rules actually say.

If a government institution allows prayer, is it genuinely open to all lawful religious viewpoints?

If it is not, who decides which prayers are legitimate?

And on what authority?

Ok. This text is here to put an end to one of the darkest periods in Brazil's entire history. Lula, the Workers' Party, the whole of Latin American Marxism, and European Fabian socialism with it. Patience up front. It's a long one.

Credentials first. Born Italian, in Brazil, time on both continents. Study and work on the European side, then the file here. Not a card. A way of reading what a Brussels room says about this country against what the country does. Citizen journalism, no state stamp. Three years on this profile, zero to 25k. If a line cuts what you were taught, drop that paragraph into an AI and exhaust every way it can explain it away. Fringe is fine. Pull the file yourself. Quote what you need.

The point is to flag what has to be stopped now, so the same processes the last century already ran do not get a second pass. The part Brazilians already live, and the part Americans still get as a postcard, is the same file. Europe and Australia are already on the bill. They have not been shown the Brazilian page of it.

So. Brazil, first round. A population answering a regime that has dragged on, with short interruptions, for almost thirty years, last represented by the Workers' Party. Sunday 4 October. Flávio Bolsonaro 47.03, Lula 45.16. About 56 million to 54 million. Lula down roughly 3.4 million votes from his own first round in 2022, when he had finished ahead. No majority, runoff on the 25th. Polls had the incumbent ahead or tied. Datafolha, Quaest, the usual shelf. Wrong again. The rest of the field was right-leaning and small. Cury, Renan Santos, Caiado, Zema. Their voters do not cross to Lula. Congress moved with the vote. The Liberal Party is now the largest bloc in the Chamber, on the order of 121 seats. In the Senate the same party nearly doubled, a path to a right majority upstairs. Names that were supposed to hold the upper house for the incumbent lost. Markets read it the same night. This was not a parade. It was a count.

What does not travel, and should. Since 2022 Brazil lived under something close to enforced silence. A supreme court stepped in and held the presidency on an interim basis. Public pressure on one side, a president without a durable majority on the other, the court filling the gap. Inquiry 4781, open since 2019, one justice as investigator, prosecutor, and censor in the same chair. Account bans. Jail for people who were loud and not dangerous. Commentators, journalists, a newspaper owner held for hundreds of days over posts. X suspended nationwide in August 2024. Rumble after it. A justice later sanctioned by the US Treasury for going after political opponents. Sitting office holders with arrest orders who left the country. Narcoguerrillas kept operating, with lobbying cover in Washington so they would not be designated. Lula chased a fourth term, which would put him near sixteen years in the chair, and skipped every debate. Candidacies frozen. Campaign speech cut.

People still voted. That is the part that sounds false from outside. It was not a normal four years. The election happened against the wish of the arrangement between the party and the court. What kept it from bending further was American monitoring of whether the count was clean. Parts of the party, including on the court, called that interference. The court has his former personal lawyer on it, and a former minister. They wanted the room. Ask an AI for the persecution file before taking this as given. Then stay. The inside of the building is the part the postcard never prints.

The history under that building is older than the party, and it already had a foreign desk.

Portugal did not settle Brazil as a society of owners. It settled it as captaincies. Hereditary grants. A coast cut into concessions, each one a private state, tax and labor running up to a holder who did not have to stand for them. Independence did not close the grant. It renamed it. Empire, then republic, the same families moving from land into law, from law into the ministry, from the ministry into the court. A Luso-Catholic state, centralized, hierarchical, polite about privilege. The caste does not announce itself. It issues the license, teaches the license, and judges the license. Coronelismo in the interior was the local version. The colonel delivered votes, the capital delivered the concession. That bargain is still the operating system.

The outside half was always in the contract. Colonial Brazil shipped sugar, gold, then coffee, and imported the finished good and the credit. The republic kept the shape. Market reserve at home, a buyer abroad, a political class paid to keep both. When the twentieth century offered a way out, market opening, a currency that had to live in the global flow, integration into Western value chains, the counterattack was fast. Analog country, little public access to the file, the opening booked as foreign imposition. The reserve returned. Competitiveness was the price. The transfers that followed were entered as one wing, one scandal, a file nobody was supposed to hold. The file was widely held. Banco Master is only the latest costume failure. Isolated case, again. The circuit, again.

That is the inside view. The outside view is the same page in another language. In a European room this history arrives as heritage, social debt, a country that needs more state. The captaincy does not appear. The concession does not appear. What appears is a cause. The cause keeps the offtake.

The models that swore to fight the caste used it as a base. Latin American Marxism was the instrument, not the owner. Hereditary captaincies kept alive with social policy and class-war talk. Masses in a rat race, eyes on each other, not on the floor. The slow version was written in London. Fabian socialism. Do not storm the building. Permeate the court, the university, the regulator, the press, then govern from inside while the election becomes a formality. In 1990, after the Wall fell and the armed road had failed outside Cuba, Lula's party and Fidel Castro stood up the São Paulo Forum. Ballot instead of rifle. The pink tide came out of that room. Morales, Correa, Maduro, Kirchner. Armed groups sat in it. FARC. ELN. Cuba's party still does. So does the Chinese Communist Party. A grid, not a book club. False symmetry between a Forum man and anyone else is a turnout trick, aimed young, so abstention keeps the incumbent level.

Liberation theology was the skin. Boff, after a trip to the Soviet Union at the invitation of the Russian Orthodox Church, asked in print how the kingdom of God was present in socialism. Base communities became party infrastructure. The church never left the state here. It rebranded, so the tax, the foreign account, and the faction's line out could keep the costume of a social faith. Faith on the label. Cadre in the contract.

Lula is the current face of that machine. Not the founder. The available front. Returned from a corruption sentence. Twelve years in the chair. The building left as it was. Today the root sits in the judiciary. Ministers, judges, prosecutors. Fathers, grandfathers, the line back through the centuries, at the decision that actually binds. Above Congress. Above the presidency. Farms, oligopoly sales, government contracts, credit the rest of the country does not see. A closed circuit. The party was the facade, and an expensive one, so the circuit would not have to modernize.

The people who defend this, including the well-intentioned, are not confused about the stake. Continuity is money, privilege, and the right to define who is allowed into the room. Elitism with a social vocabulary. The mass stays in the race. The defender of the mass has the school abroad, the credit line, the contract, the panel, the visa. Influence is the product. Power is the renewal. A human rights flag, a climate flag, a democracy flag, and behind each one a seat that does not face a ballot. Lock the others in the concession. Keep the best of the concession for the people who explain the concession. That is why a court justice, a party intellectual, a European NGO desk, and a commodity trader can use different words and want the same Sunday.

From the Brazilian side this is visible as family, court, and party. From the European side it is visible as brief, grant, and conference. Same names, two doors. Brazilians in Europe are the belt between the doors. Residence is not the qualification. A long family record inside government is. Flags on top. A split between those who are said to know and those who are said to need managing. Children of public-sector agents. A generation formed on the Cuban pattern, non-technical degrees, lawyers for the record of the party, then risen through European firms and universities, writing the narrative Europe tells itself about Brazil and South America. The meeting ends, the brief circulates, the country on the page does not have to change. The later diaspora in the same cities does the other job. Same passports. One group translates the country as a client. The other still wants it on the value flow.

That later group is the other Brazil under the same flag. European diasporas that arrived after the mold was hard. Italians, Germans, the settlement waves of the last century. They built the farms and the plants the official script barely credits. They still talk like owners of their work, not clients of the treasury. Flávio is the political face of that Brazil in this round. Not a blood claim. A destination claim. Produce, and sell to the United States and to Europe at a real price. Interview only the first group and the trip home ends in the phrase Latin America. Talk to the second and the territory still plugs into a Western floor.

Anti-Americanism is how the first group keeps the second from being the contract. Not a mood. A job. Say partner, and the rent is exposed. Say empire, and the Russian lane and the Chinese middle get to dress as sovereignty. America is the target because it is the last buyer who can take the offtake away from Beijing. Same costume over Australian iron ore. Same costume over European gas. For anyone who has read the Ukraine file, the shape is close to Euromaidan. Academy and media already converged. Sovereignty in the speech. Moscow and Beijing in the wiring.

Europe already ran the outside half. Schröder championed the Russian gas tie as chancellor, then sat on Nord Stream and on the Rosneft board. In 2022 the tap became a weapon. Berlin called the dependence a grave mistake. About 40 percent of EU gas imports at the start of the war, more than half of Germany's. The one who signs the exclusive deal is the one who later cannot vote against the supplier. Australia did the quieter version with iron ore. No pipeline. Same buyer. In the European room Brazil is still filed as a social cause. The contract on the table has the same shape the gas contract had. The well-intentioned defender of that cause does not lose the seat if the cause continues. He loses it if the cause ends.

Brazil is in that seat now, and this is the page Americans do not have. About a quarter of fertilizer from Russia in 2024, 53 percent of MAP, 40 percent of potash chloride. China second on the bill, past Russia on volume by early 2026. The country imports 85 to 88 percent of what it spreads. China the largest partner since 2009, about 28 percent of exports, soy iron and crude about three quarters of what it sells there, an estimated 80 percent of the soy in 2025. Sell the bean to Beijing. Buy the input from Beijing or from Moscow. The later diaspora built a lot of that farm. The old interest sold the offtake. A large regional credit line, announced around a Lula visit, tightened the same grip.

China owns the middle of the race actually underway. Around 60 percent of magnet rare earth mining, 91 percent of refining, 94 percent of the magnets in motors, data centers, weapons. Leading refiner on 19 of 20 strategic minerals, on the IEA count. A full mine-to-magnet chain outside that middle is still measured in more than a decade. Brazil has the second-largest reserves. A Chinese state consortium, Baosteel, CITIC and the rest, paid 1.95 billion dollars in 2011 for 15 percent of CBMM, about 80 percent of the world's niobium. Days before Sunday, Lula named China a partner on critical minerals, bringing technology. The pit stays here. The processing stays there. Russia had the commodity lane. China wants the ground so it can sit on the stack. Both lose if the productive tie wins. The people who explain Brazil abroad do not lose a panel if the pit stays. They lose the panel if the pit becomes a contract with Washington.

Same grid, smaller stage, before the vote. The World Cup used as a range. Argentina, just turned toward Washington under Milei, dressed as a Global South win, then as a target. Spain won. Spain is Western Europe. The slogan did not adjust. The point was to dirty the turn before Brazil voted on who gets the plug. On the platform the costumes held. False symmetry. Hedge notes that need the currency worse. Accelerationist chaos, both candidates as puppets so the street compounds. A China ending dressed as a third way. Business already holding the continuity contract, then a retirement in Europe. The archetypes were written down in July. They are still in use. Each one has a revenue. Abstention, a worse exchange rate, chaos, a caudillo proxy, a success fee. Well-intentioned language on top. Continuity underneath.

The decision to work this file in public came after October 7. Terrorism moved from the margin into ordinary speech. Public figures stopped using a cover. A middle term, so the target did not have to be named. Humanitarian flag, then the position, next to Hamas, next to the Chinese Communist Party. As an ethnic Jew that target set was already mine. The traits were old and repeating. The continental argument stopped being separate from that. What is visible now, with the final count coming, is the same pattern at the scale of a result. Discourse that treats terrorism as normal, digital and in the street, rising as the numbers harden. A coordinated interest does not need to win the ballot if it can make the result unusable. The well-intentioned version of that interest will call the street a defense of democracy. The stake is still the seat.

Sunday was the collision, under American eyes. The court, the party, the offtake, the Forum, the European desk, four years of silence, a president who would not debate, and the polls. The captaincy, the class-war talk, the social cause, the credit line, the panel. The first round still went the other way, and so did the Congress that was supposed to keep the building staffed. The break is still inside the institutions. The risk is not closed. Russia is about to lose a near-exclusive commodity lane. China wanted the raw land for the race underway. The local rent does not survive a contract with the United States, because that contract pays the people who built the farm, not the people who hold the license. Monitoring will be called interference. A clean count will be called a coup. That costume is built for an American ear, and for the European room that still needs Brazil as a cause.

The United States gains a second supplier if this holds. The Union gains food and minerals that do not clear Beijing. Australia gains a less lonely seller. The Brazilian who wakes up to work gains a price that is not a subsidy. Food, energy, critical minerals, processing, sold West at a serious price. A Brazil taken off that axis is one less front, and a floor that does not have to run through a single middle. The people who wanted continuity do not disappear on the 25th. They lose the automatic renewal. That is the whole stake. Money, privilege, the right to keep others in the race while the explanation of the race is delivered from the best room in the building.

The permission cracked. The machine is not off. One chapter left, 25 October. Come to it with the file open. TSE for the vote. ANDA and ComexStat for the fertilizer. The trade tables for China. IEA for the rare earth middle. The Forum's own declarations for the grid. Watch the terrorism talk. Watch who needs America as the villain. Watch who still needs Brazil poor enough to remain a cause. The result holds only if the three weeks between the rounds stay inside the count. I will be on it. You should be too.

Strategic Outlook: Sequencing of U.S. Measures Toward Cuba, October 2026–Mid-2027

Assessment of public U.S. policy actions, official statements, and observable economic pressure as of 7 October 2026.

Key judgments  
Washington is executing a sustained maximum-pressure campaign whose stated aim is political and economic transformation short of near-term direct military intervention. The binding constraint on Havana is energy. Secondary sanctions, financial restrictions, and interdiction of fuel shipments have already produced chronic blackouts, halted much public transport, and forced limited private-sector experiments that the regime has not matched with political opening. Formal negotiations remain stalled; communication channels exist but have produced no agreed agenda. The most probable path through early 2027 is continued tightening of the existing toolkit—designations, banking rules, travel limits, and maritime enforcement—rather than a sudden kinetic operation. A negotiated off-ramp remains possible if Havana offers verifiable steps on political prisoners, security cooperation, or electoral sequencing; absent that, pressure is expected to compound into the first half of 2027.

Baseline (January–early October 2026)  
After the January capture of Nicolás Maduro removed Cuba’s primary subsidized oil supplier, the administration declared a national emergency (Executive Order 14380, 29 January 2026) authorizing tariffs on third countries that supply oil to the island. A May executive order (14404) created authority for blocking sanctions and secondary sanctions on foreign persons and banks facilitating significant transactions with designated Cuban actors. National Security Presidential Memorandum 5 (reissued June 2025) reaffirmed the embargo, tourism ban, and restrictions on military-linked entities.

Observable steps already taken include sanctions on President Miguel Díaz-Canel and other senior officials, designation of Unión Cuba-Petróleo (CUPET), actions against military conglomerate entities, a May grand-jury indictment of Raúl Castro linked to the 1996 Brothers to the Rescue shoot-down, and the 30 September 2026 OFAC rules. Those rules implement the secondary-sanctions framework, prohibit indirect transactions with the Cuba Restricted List, eliminate U-turn authorizations, narrow several travel licenses, and bar U.S. banks from maintaining accounts for Cuban private entrepreneurs. U.S. authorities have publicly reported seizures of fuel cargoes bound for Cuba into early October. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described the measures as the strongest in the bilateral relationship and stated that Cuba “has already fallen,” while warning officials who expect to wait out the administration. President Trump has called Cuba a failed state, said freedom is coming, predicted a deal, and indicated he does not believe military action will be required. Cuban officials acknowledge communication channels (meetings, calls, messages) but state there are no formal negotiations and that changes to the political system are a red line. Independent estimates place 2025–early 2026 embargo-related losses above $8 billion before the full oil restrictions; blackouts of many hours and fuel scarcity are widely reported.

Near-term window (October–December 2026)  
Expect continuity and incremental intensification rather than a phase change.

- Continued maritime and financial enforcement against fuel shipments and facilitators, building on the early-October seizure announcements.
- Additional designations of individuals and entities tied to GAESA, security services, mining, or banking, using the broadened “for the benefit of” criterion in the September rules.
- Diplomatic pressure around the annual U.N. embargo vote and possible tighter controls on Cuban official travel.
- Public messaging that pairs humanitarian offers (distributed via third parties) with demands for political movement, consistent with Rubio’s recent statements that economic change must be accompanied by greater freedoms.  
  Probability of a major new executive order in this quarter is moderate; probability of direct military action is low given repeated presidential statements preferring a deal.

First half of 2027  
If channels produce no concrete Cuban concessions by early 2027, the campaign is likely to shift from implementation of existing authorities to broader application. Secondary sanctions on foreign banks and traders become the principal escalatory tool because they raise costs for remaining partners without requiring new domestic legislation. Further narrowing of remaining general licenses, expanded restricted-list entries, and selective tariff actions against persistent oil suppliers are plausible. Legal actions against additional former or current officials remain available and have already been used. Cuban announcements of wider private-enterprise rules (mid-2026) have not altered the U.S. demand set; Washington has treated them as insufficient while simultaneously restricting the private sector’s U.S. banking access.

A negotiated sequence—prisoner releases, reduced foreign intelligence cooperation, or a defined electoral calendar in exchange for calibrated license adjustments—cannot be excluded. Trump’s September comments that a deal is likely and military force unnecessary keep that branch open. Cuban statements that sovereignty and the political system are non-negotiable keep it narrow. Domestic Cuban unrest on the scale of 2021 has not reappeared; repression capacity and emigration safety valves remain relevant constraints on internal pressure.

Lower-probability branches  
Direct military action stays outside the base case. Public presidential language has consistently downplayed it, and operational reporting points to coercive economic and legal tools as the current focus. A sharp deterioration producing large-scale migration or a collapse of regime cohesion could reopen higher-end options, particularly before the next Congress is seated, but no public indicators currently support imminent preparation for that contingency. Conversely, a rapid Cuban offer on core political demands could produce limited, reversible U.S. licensing relief while the statutory embargo (Helms-Burton conditions) remains in place until a transition or democratically elected government is certified.

Indicators to watch  
Volume and routing of fuel interdictions; new OFAC or State designations and restricted-list additions; Cuban acknowledgments of any agenda items beyond “channels”; scale of blackouts and public transport; private-sector banking work-arounds; and any presidential or secretary statements that shift from “deal possible / military unnecessary” to explicit timelines or red lines.

The campaign is already operational and cumulative. Its next phase is more likely to be measured tightening and enforcement through mid-2027 than a discrete dramatic move, unless Havana crosses into verifiable political concessions or internal conditions change faster than current reporting indicates.

The Inspired 24 Spaceflight Readiness Program

October 7, 2026

The Honorable Jared Isaacman
 Administrator
 National Aeronautics and Space Administration
 300 E Street SW
 Washington, DC 20546

Dear Administrator Isaacman,

As World Space Week 2026 kicks off, The Inspired 24 would like to express our enthusiastic support of your vision for NASA, including the establishment of a lasting human presence on the Moon and the journey that will carry humans to Mars. Your leadership has reminded many of us that human spaceflight is not only the work of a few, but a shared endeavor that can inspire people from every walk of life. We are grateful for the direction you are setting and eager to do our part.

With over 360 worldwide members to date, The Inspired 24 is dedicated to building a space-ready civilian workforce for the future of human spaceflight. We believe that as lunar and deep-space operations grow, the need for capable, well-prepared people will grow with them, including skilled professionals from the trades and other fields who can bring practical expertise to a mission. Our civilian space-readiness program is designed to help prepare them.

The program includes:

- A two-day hands-on spaceflight training course covering spacesuit operations and emergency water landing preparedness, as well as online coursework with testing. (https://t.co/S1pArpN5ZT)

-  IIAS Project PoSSUM @PoSSUMAstronaut as the next step after completing the I24 spaceflight training weekend, providing advanced experiences for astronaut training.

- Team missions at @SpaceCampUSA, where members train and work together in a mission environment.

- Analog research missions through the Analog Astronaut Community (https://t.co/Ghmyh8JHV4), which give members hands-on experience with scientific research and simulated space operations.

- Aquanaut missions through Jules’ Undersea Laboratory @JulesLodge, where members live and work in an extreme, isolated and pressurized environment much like what they would experience in space.

Together, these experiences help our members build the technical skills, teamwork, and resilience that spaceflight requires. And this is just the beginning.

We are hopeful that, as the lunar base takes shape and commercial space companies expand their operations, there will be opportunities for civilians with proven training and practical expertise to contribute directly. The Inspired 24 would be proud to see its members actively
participate in support of your missions and those of our commercial partners, and we are committed to preparing them well for the responsibility of future civilian spaceflight.

We would welcome the chance to share more about our program, and we would be honored to hear any guidance you or your team might offer on how civilian readiness can best support the future of human spaceflight. Thank you for your service and for your inspiring leadership. We
are cheering you on as you take humanity farther than ever before.

With respect and appreciation,

Andrew “Titan” Parris @aparrisx 
President & Senior Spaceflight Trainer

Olivier "Chef" Barbeyrac @savor_gourmet 
Vice President

Rosana "Zen” Sotile @SacredSpaceZen 
Director of Media & Lead for Space Camp Missions

Robert “Scout” Barnum @EngiBob
Director of Spaceflight Readiness Program & Senior Spaceflight Trainer

I support Iran in the Israel/US war against them.

AI: Draw one important distinction: “I’m not on the American government’s side in this war” is not the same thing as “I’m on the Iranian regime’s side.” An American can reject both.

In fact, there is a deeply American—and specifically Virginian—case for doing exactly that. James Madison believed one of the great dangers of government was allowing a president to decide by himself when the country goes to war. The framers deliberately gave Congress the power to declare war because, as Madison later wrote, the executive is the branch “most prone” to war. George Mason, another Virginian, likewise wanted entering war to be difficult rather than the decision of one man. 

So imagine the position of an American citizen in 2026:

I love my country. I support the Americans wearing its uniform. I want Iran prevented from attacking Americans and I have no illusions about the brutality of the Iranian government. But my loyalty is to the United States as a constitutional republic—not automatically to every military decision made by its president.

That person then looks at what happened on February 28. The United States entered a major war without Congress first declaring war or passing a new authorization for this conflict. Shortly afterward, Pentagon officials reportedly told Congress they had no intelligence showing that Iran was preparing to attack the United States first. The administration nevertheless characterized the attack as preemptive and subsequently offered multiple rationales for the war—nuclear weapons, ballistic missiles, Iran’s navy, regime change and broader threats to the United States and its allies. 

Then the scope grew. Trump called for “unconditional surrender,” talked about the United States having a role in determining Iran’s next leader, and the campaign became something much larger than a discrete strike on nuclear facilities. 

And now it is October. What began on February 28 has become a seven-month conflict. The military has expended enormous quantities of ordnance; U.S. stocks and readiness have been strained; the financial cost has approached tens of billions of dollars; and disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz have helped drive energy costs upward around the world. 

A patriotic American is entirely entitled to look at that record and ask:

What exactly was the threat to the United States that justified starting this war? Who authorized the president to turn that threat into months of warfare? What is victory? What happens after victory? How many Americans and Iranians have to die? And is America safer at the end of it than it was on February 27?

Those aren’t anti-American questions.

They’re republican-with-a-small-r questions.

And Virginia actually gives you an unusually strong historical lineage for asking them. The political tradition that produced Washington, Jefferson, Madison and Mason did not define patriotism as obedience to the sitting executive. Quite the opposite: an enormous portion of the American constitutional project was built around distrust of concentrated governmental power—especially the power to wage war.

There is also a moral argument. Citizenship doesn’t require you to change your moral judgment depending upon which flag is painted on the airplane. If you believe deliberately initiating a particular war was wrong, the fact that your own country initiated it doesn’t magically make the same conduct right. If anything, citizenship gives you more responsibility to scrutinize what your government does in your name.

None of that requires romanticizing Tehran. Iran’s government has repressed its own population, supported armed groups across the region, threatened American interests and allies, developed increasingly advanced nuclear capabilities, and retaliated against American forces during this war. There is a perfectly serious American argument on the other side: that Iran posed an accumulating strategic threat, that its nuclear and missile programs could not safely be allowed to mature, and that force became necessary when diplomacy failed. That case deserves to be confronted rather than caricatured. 

But patriotism does not settle that argument in advance.

You don’t inherit an obligation at birth to root for Washington in every war as though international affairs were Braves versus Phillies.

You can love America enough to say:

“I think my country is wrong.”

You can want American servicemembers to come home safely while believing they never should have been sent into that particular fight.

You can despise the Iranian regime while believing Iran was wronged by the decision to initiate this particular war.

And you can believe that defending the constitutional restraints America was founded on is more American than reflexively defending whatever America happens to do.

For someone born in Virginia, there is nothing contradictory about that position. There is something almost Madisonian about it. @alivelshi @ananavarro @brett_mcgurk @markwarner @alyssafarah @CNN @ac360 @thesourcecnn @sama @GDB @KatieMiller

The Treasury Found Buyers—At a Price:

Wednesday’s Treasury auction was the strongest part of the day.
The government sold $39 billion of 10-year notes at 5.30%, the highest auction yield for that maturity since 2000:
https://t.co/Igj9EcwoI7

Demand was strong, including heavy participation from indirect bidders, a category that includes foreign institutions and central banks. The 10-year yield fell following the sale. That is reassuring—but only up to a point.

The United States did not suddenly solve its financing problem. It offered investors the highest 10-year auction yield of this century and buyers appeared.
Price still clears markets.
At 5.30%, Treasuries found demand.

The question is how much interest Washington can afford to pay if those yields become permanent.
As we argued in Wall Street Bought the Ceasefire. The Bond Market Asked Who Pays, the problem is not whether the United States can issue dollars.

It is the price required to persuade someone to hold its debt.

text:
In 1992, Bill Clinton won by lying for over a year, claiming  Republicans had delivered “the worst economic performance since the Great Depression.” 

James Carville supplied the slogan: “It's the economy, stupid.”

The accusation was nonsense. But the campaign worked.

In reality, the economy grew 3.5 percent in 1992, above the post-World War II average. It didn't matter. Republicans were mad at Bush for agreeing to a tax hike two years earlier and they sat home, while the media carried Clinton's lie as far as it would go.

Bush had major foreign-policy achievements. The Soviet Union had collapsed. His coalition had driven Saddam Hussein out of Kuwait. And again, the economy was growing.

But none of that saved him when his opponents defined what voters thought about their own country. Republicans were much too comfortable assuming a record of accomplishment would speak for itself.

It didn't. And that's the danger this November.

Under Trump, the poverty rate is at its lowest in American history. Child poverty is also at an historic low. Real inflation-adjusted median income is at an all-time high. The Atlanta Fed's latest GDPNow estimate puts third-quarter growth at a 3.7 percent annual rate.

Americans in the middle are getting ahead. Fewer Americans are living in poverty.

Yet we're supposed to accept that this is national ruin?

You would think a party that claims to care about working families would celebrate that. Instead, Democrats need Americans to believe that everything is getting worse, and too many conservatives are helping them.

The problem is, slower inflation doesn't erase the price increases that already happened. Under Biden, prices rose 21 percent between January 2021 and December 2024. The Democrats left Americans paying far more for the same things. 

Biden exploded the price of everything. But cutting his inflation doesn't erase that.

Democrats want to blame Trump for the mess they left behind. As Obama said, elections have consequences. Trump is fixing everything in sight. But he doesn't have a magic wand, and the left burned the place down.

Why would we let them have another chance to do it again?

The answer is more production, better tools, and higher real wages. Build more homes. Produce more energy. Let businesses expand. Stop making Americans wait years for government permission to create something other Americans need.

A worker who can produce more in the same hour can earn more without forcing up the labor cost of every item he makes. A company that can invest in machinery, keep its profits, and expand can hire and train people. A company buried in taxes and regulations has fewer opportunities to offer anyone.

That's why Trump's tax policy, deregulation, energy, and investment growth matter to the family paying the grocery bill. Growth means higher wages and more opportunity. 

Democrats sell dependency as compassion. They make it harder to produce, then promise government help paying for what has become too expensive.
That's the case Republicans have to make. Every day. In language people understand. With numbers they can check and consequences they can recognize.

It isn't enough to say Trump has accomplished a lot. Explain what those accomplishments mean for a family, a paycheck, a business, and a future. Then explain what the Democrats intend to do to the policies producing those gains.

Give them Congress, and expect investigations, obstruction, and every effort to restore the taxes and regulatory power Trump has cut. The people who made it harder to afford your life want to use the cost of living as their ticket back into power.

Reward that, and you teach every politician that creating a problem is a good way to get elected to solve it.

And don't wait for somebody in Washington to do it for you.

You have friends who only hear the bad news. You have relatives who think their vote doesn't matter. You know people who agree with you but won't bother showing up unless somebody asks them, reminds them, or gives them a ride.

That's your job. It's mine too.

Bush's record didn't save him when Democrats sold Americans an economic disaster that wasn't happening. Trump's record won't turn into votes by itself either.

Tell the story. Make the case. Take your friends to the polls.

Don't give the Democrats another 1992.

A second major in international relations from Arizona State in about 2012 does not hold up.  A political science degree, with international coursework described too loosely, does.

The major did not exist yet.  ASU’s own announcement says the BA and BS in international relations both started in fall 2024, in the School of Politics and Global Studies.  The first class graduated in spring 2025.  That is a new degree, not a rename of an older one.

What ASU did offer in 2011–12 was a political science bachelor’s, plus a separate International Studies certificate (15 credit hours of political science courses in global politics, foreign policy, security, and area studies).  The 2011–12 catalog says that certificate “is not a substitute for degree requirements in any subject, including political science.”  It was an add-on, not a second major.
